Cumulative, beginner-facing, grouped by the book chapter where each term is introduced (not A–Z). Each entry is one sentence plus a link to the section that introduces it. A later chapter may add a stricter sense of a term, but the original entry stays.

## Chapter 1

- **ML system.** The whole production setup around a model: requirements, interfaces, data stack, the logic for developing, deploying, monitoring, and updating models, and the infrastructure that runs it. See [Chapter 1, What an ML system is](lectures/week01.qmd#sec-ml-system).
- **MLOps.** The tools and best practices for bringing ML into production (deploying, monitoring, maintaining). See [Chapter 1, What an ML system is](lectures/week01.qmd#sec-ml-system).
- **ML systems design.** A system approach to MLOps that treats all components and stakeholders as a whole so they meet the stated objectives. See [Chapter 1, What an ML system is](lectures/week01.qmd#sec-ml-system).
- **Five-part test.** ML learns complex patterns from existing data to make predictions on unseen data; a problem should satisfy each part before ML is used. See [Chapter 1, The five-part test](lectures/week01.qmd#sec-five-part).
- **Zero-shot learning.** Predicting on a task with no training data for that task, by relying on training for related tasks. See [Chapter 1, The five-part test](lectures/week01.qmd#sec-five-part).
- **i.i.d. assumption.** Training and future data are drawn independently from the same distribution; ML's usefulness on unseen data depends on it roughly holding. See [Chapter 1, The five-part test](lectures/week01.qmd#sec-five-part).
- **Distribution shift.** The serving data distribution differs from the training distribution. See [Chapter 1, The five-part test](lectures/week01.qmd#sec-five-part); monitored in Chapter 8.
- **Concept drift.** The pattern relating inputs to outputs changes over time, so fixed rules or models go stale. See [Chapter 1, When ML shines](lectures/week01.qmd#sec-shines).
- **Ensembling.** Combining several learning algorithms to beat any one of them; common in competitions, less common in production because of latency and interpretability costs. See [Chapter 1, Stakeholders and requirements](lectures/week01.qmd#sec-stakeholders).
- **Latency.** Time from sending a query to receiving its result (this book uses it to mean response time). See [Chapter 1, Computational priorities](lectures/week01.qmd#sec-compute).
- **Throughput.** Number of queries processed per unit time; with sequential batches, batch size divided by time per batch. See [Chapter 1, Latency and throughput under batching](lectures/week01.qmd#sec-batching).
- **Percentile (p50, p90, p99).** The value below which roughly that percentage of measurements fall; p50 is the median. Used for latency targets; tail percentiles need many samples to be stable. See [Chapter 1, Latency is a distribution](lectures/week01.qmd#sec-percentiles).
- **Algorithmic bias.** Systematic model error that disadvantages a group, often inherited from training data and amplified by scale. See [Chapter 1, Fairness](lectures/week01.qmd#sec-fairness).
- **Interpretability.** How far people can understand why a model produced an output; needed for user trust, bias detection, and debugging. See [Chapter 1, Interpretability](lectures/week01.qmd#sec-interpretability).
- **Data poisoning.** Planting training examples to manipulate a model's behaviour. See [Chapter 1, ML systems versus traditional software](lectures/week01.qmd#sec-vs-software).

## Chapter 2

- **Business objective vs ML objective.** What the organization wants (revenue, retention) versus a measurable property of the model (accuracy, latency); the second matters only through the first. See [Chapter 2, Business and ML objectives](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-objectives).
- **Take-rate.** Netflix's recommender metric: quality plays divided by recommendations seen, used as a bridge to business metrics. See [Chapter 2, Business and ML objectives](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-objectives).
- **Reliability.** Keeping the correct function at the desired performance despite faults; ML systems can fail silently. See [Chapter 2, Reliability](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-reliability).
- **Scalability.** Reasonable ways to handle growth in model complexity, traffic, and model count, through resource scaling and artifact management. See [Chapter 2, Scalability](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-scalability).
- **Autoscaling.** Automatically adding or removing machines as usage changes. See [Chapter 2, Scalability](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-scalability).
- **Maintainability.** Structuring work so mixed teams can use their own tools, with documented, versioned, reproducible code, data, and models. See [Chapter 2, Maintainability](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-maintainability).
- **Adaptability.** Finding where to improve and updating without service interruption, to keep up with shifting data and requirements. See [Chapter 2, Adaptability](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-adaptability).
- **ML problem.** A problem defined by its inputs, outputs, and objective function. See [Chapter 2, Framing ML problems](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-framing).
- **Classification vs regression.** Predicting a category versus a continuous value; each can be reframed as the other (bucketing, or a probability plus a threshold). See [Chapter 2, Classification versus regression](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-class-vs-reg).
- **Decision threshold.** The cutoff that turns a predicted score or probability into a class; it need not be 0.5. See [Chapter 2, Classification versus regression](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-class-vs-reg).
- **High cardinality.** A classification task with a very large number of classes, which makes collecting enough examples of rare classes hard. See [Chapter 2, Binary versus multiclass classification](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-binary-multiclass).
- **Hierarchical classification.** Classifying first into a coarse group, then into a subgroup with a second classifier. See [Chapter 2, Binary versus multiclass classification](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-binary-multiclass).
- **Multilabel classification.** Each example can belong to several classes at once, encoded as a multi-hot vector. See [Chapter 2, Multiclass versus multilabel classification](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-multilabel).
- **Objective (loss) function.** The function training minimizes, comparing predictions with labels; distinct from a business or ML objective. See [Chapter 2, Objective functions](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-objective-functions).
- **Cross-entropy.** $-\sum_i p_i \log q_i$; with a one-hot label, minus the log of the probability on the true class. Log loss is the binary case. See [Chapter 2, Objective functions](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-objective-functions).
- **Decoupling objectives.** Training one model per objective and combining their scores, so trade-offs can be retuned without retraining. See [Chapter 2, Decoupling objectives](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-decoupling).
